new_note: *Then give place to the physician, for Yahuah (God) has created him: let him not go from you, for you have need of him.* (Ecclesiasticus 38:12). *But Yahusha (Jesus) turned him about, and when he saw her, he said, Daughter, be of good comfort; thy faith hath made thee whole. And the woman was made whole from that hour.* (Matthew 9:22). Sirach does not slight the physician; he says Yahuah (God) created him and tells the sick man to keep him close. The woman with the issue of blood did exactly that for twelve years, and Mark 5:26 adds that she spent all she had on physicians and only grew worse. When she reached for the hem of his garment she was reaching past the physician to the one who made the physician, and Yahusha (Jesus) does not rebuke the years she spent under their care; he names her faith as what made her whole. The physician is a gift from his hand, and the healing was always his.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 38:12 — *give place to the physician, for Yahuah (God) has created him.* The bleeding woman gave place to physicians for twelve years; at Matthew 9:22 she reached past them to the one who made them, and her faith made her whole.

new_note: *For they shall also pray to Yahuah (God), that he would prosper that, which they give for ease and remedy to prolong life.* (Ecclesiasticus 38:14). *But when the people were put forth, he went in, and took her by the hand, and the maid arose.* (Matthew 9:25). Sirach says the physician himself prays to Yahuah (God) that the remedy in his hand would prosper, because the healing never belonged to the remedy. In the ruler's house the remedies have run out; the girl is dead, and no physician prays over a corpse. Yahusha (Jesus) walks in and takes her by the hand, and the one the physician prays to is the one standing in the room. The physician asks for the prospering; here the giver of it does the work with his own hand.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 38:14 — *they shall also pray to Yahuah (God), that he would prosper that, which they give.* The physician prays that his remedy would prosper; at Matthew 9:25 the one he prays to takes the dead girl by the hand himself.

new_note: *When the great Yahuah (God) will, he shall be filled with the spirit of understanding: he shall pour out wise sentences, and give thanks to Yahuah (God) in his prayer.* (Ecclesiasticus 39:6). *But blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear.* (Matthew 13:16). Sirach says the scribe is filled with the spirit of understanding when the great Yahuah (God) wills it; the man does not work it up out of his own study, he is filled. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the disciples their eyes and ears are blessed, and the verse before explains why: *it is given unto you to know the mysteries of the kingdom* (Matthew 13:11). The seeing and the hearing are given the same way the scribe's understanding is given. The hand that fills the scribe is the hand that opens the disciple's eyes, and both of them answer with thanks.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 39:6 — *he shall be filled with the spirit of understanding: he shall pour out wise sentences.* Understanding is given when Yahuah (God) wills; the blessed eyes and ears of Matthew 13:16 are given the same way.

new_note: *Great travail is created for every man, and an heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mother’s womb, till the day that they return to the mother of all things.* (Ecclesiasticus 40:1). *Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble.* (Job 14:1). Job and Sirach are looking at the same life. Job says the man born of a woman has few days and all of them full of trouble; Sirach says the heavy yoke lies on the sons of Adam from the day they leave the womb until the day they go back into the earth that is the mother of all things. Neither one is complaining about bad luck. They are describing the sentence laid on Adam in the garden, sorrow all his days and a return to the dust (Genesis 3:17–19), carried down the line to every son born of him.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 40:1 — *an heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mother’s womb.* Job 14:1 says the same of the man born of a woman: few days, full of trouble, the yoke laid on Adam carried down his line.

new_note: *By his counsel he appeaseth the deep, and planteth islands in it.* (Ecclesiasticus 43:23). *And in the fourth watch of the night Yahusha (Jesus) went unto them, walking on the sea.* (Matthew 14:25). Sirach praises the Maker who stills the deep by his counsel and sets islands in it, and Job says of the same one that he *alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea* (Job 9:8). In the fourth watch of the night the disciples watch a man do what Job said belongs to Elohim (God) alone. The one whose counsel appeases the deep is walking across it. The one who spoke the sea into its bounds came in flesh and treads on his own work.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 43:23 — *By his counsel he appeaseth the deep, and planteth islands in it.* The one who stills the deep by his counsel walks on it at Matthew 14:25; Job 9:8 said he alone treads upon the waves of the sea.

new_note: *For in it be strange and wondrous works, variety of all kinds of beasts and whales created.* (Ecclesiasticus 43:25). *And in the fourth watch of the night Yahusha (Jesus) went unto them, walking on the sea.* (Matthew 14:25). Sirach looks at the sea as a storehouse of the Creator's wonders, every beast and whale in it created, and in the next line he says *by his word all things consist* (Ecclesiasticus 43:26). The disciples saw a figure on the water and took it for a spirit. What they saw was the Creator of the sea walking on his own creation, and when he spoke he gave them his name, *it is I; be not afraid* (Matthew 14:27). The word that holds the sea together was the word speaking to them from on top of it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 43:25 — *in it be strange and wondrous works, variety of all kinds of beasts and whales created.* The sea is the Creator's storehouse of wonders; at Matthew 14:25 the Creator walks on it and tells them, it is I.

new_note: *All these were honoured in their generations, and were the glory of their times.* (Ecclesiasticus 44:7). *Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.* (Hebrews 11:1). Sirach's roll of honoured men and the roll of Hebrews 11 are the same men: Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, the prophets. Sirach says they were the glory of their times; Hebrews says what made them so, they held things hoped for as already theirs and lived on the evidence of what they had not yet seen. Hebrews finishes the roll by saying they all died without receiving the promise, waiting for us so that they would not be made perfect without us (Hebrews 11:39–40). The glory of their generations was a faith that is still waiting for the resurrection to be paid out.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 44:7 — *All these were honoured in their generations, and were the glory of their times.* The honoured men of Sirach 44 are the roll of Hebrews 11; the glory of their times was faith in things not yet seen.
flag: Live Hebrews 11:1 text contains the word 'substance' inside the quoted verse itself; left as scripture reads.

new_note: *Noah was found perfect and righteous; in the time of wrath he was taken in exchange for the world; therefore was he left as a remnant to the earth, when the flood came.* (Ecclesiasticus 44:17). *By faith Noah, being warned of Elohim (God) of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith.* (Hebrews 11:7). Sirach says Noah was found perfect and righteous and was left as a remnant to the earth when the flood came; Hebrews says Noah believed a warning about things not yet seen and built an ark, condemning the world by doing it. These are not two different Noahs. The righteousness Genesis saw in him, *Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations, and Noah walked with Elohim (God)* (Genesis 6:9), was faith with its hands on the timber. He is the first remnant in scripture, one household kept alive through the wrath while the world around it perished, and Sirach calls the trade by its name: he was taken in exchange for the world.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 44:17 — *Noah was found perfect and righteous; in the time of wrath he was taken in exchange for the world.* Hebrews 11:7 shows the faith behind the righteousness: Noah believed what was not yet seen and built, and was left as a remnant.

new_note: *Who kept the law of the Most High, and was in covenant with him: he established the covenant in his flesh; and when he was proved, he was found faithful.* (Ecclesiasticus 44:20). *And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, Yahuah (LORD) appeared to Abram, and said unto him, I am the El Shaddai (Almighty God); walk before me, and be thou perfect.* (Genesis 17:1). Sirach says Abraham kept the law of the Most High, and he says it of a man who lived centuries before Sinai. Genesis 17 shows what that law was: Yahuah (God) appears and commands him to walk before him and be perfect, and in the same chapter gives him the covenant in his flesh, the circumcision Sirach names (Genesis 17:10–11). When Yahuah (God) later speaks of Abraham he says he *obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws* (Genesis 26:5). The commandments did not begin with Moses; Abraham walked in them, and when he was proved on the mountain he was found faithful.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 44:20 — *Who kept the law of the Most High, and was in covenant with him.* The law Abraham kept is the walk Yahuah (God) commanded at Genesis 17:1, and the covenant in his flesh is the circumcision of the same chapter.

new_note: *Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:1). *In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judaea,* (Matthew 3:1). Sirach opens his praise of Elijah with fire: he stood up as fire and his word burned like a lamp. Matthew opens John's ministry in the wilderness, and the fire is already there in what he says, *O generation of vipers* and *he shall baptize you with the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Ghost), and with fire* (Matthew 3:7, 11). The angel had told Zacharias his son would go before Yahuah (God) in the spirit and power of Elias (Luke 1:17), and Yahusha (Jesus) later says it plainly, *this is Elias, which was for to come* (Matthew 11:14). The prophet who stood up as fire has stood up again in the wilderness of Judaea.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:1 — *Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.* John comes preaching in the wilderness at Matthew 3:1 with the same fire in his word; he is the Elijah who was to come.

new_note: *Then stood up Elias the prophet as fire, and his word burned like a lamp.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:1). *For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.* (Matthew 14:3). Elijah's fire burned hottest at the king's court. He told Ahab to his face that the house of Ahab had forsaken the commandments of Yahuah (God), and Jezebel sought his life for it. John carried the same fire to Herod's court and said *it is not lawful for thee to have her* (Matthew 14:4), the Torah spoken against the king's own bed (Leviticus 18:16). Herod answered the prophet the way Ahab's house had answered Elijah: the king turned on him and a queen wanted him dead; this time the prophet was caught and bound. The word that burns like a lamp is not dimmed for royalty, and royalty does not forgive it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:1 — *his word burned like a lamp.* Elijah's fire at Ahab's court is John's word to Herod at Matthew 14:3–4; the king answers the prophet by binding him.

new_note: *He brought a sore famine upon them, and by his zeal he diminished their number.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:2). *For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.* (Matthew 14:3). Elijah's zeal against Ahab's idolatry shut up heaven; *there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word* (1 Kings 17:1), and the famine thinned the land. John's zeal against Herod's unlawful marriage brought no famine; it brought a prison cell and, before long, his head on a platter. The zeal is the same zeal, a prophet unwilling to let a king break the Torah in peace. Sirach records what it cost Ahab's people; Matthew records what it cost the prophet. Neither man softened the word to spare himself the consequences.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:2 — *by his zeal he diminished their number.* Elijah's zeal against Ahab's court brought famine; John's zeal against Herod's court brought his imprisonment at Matthew 14:3.

new_note: *Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:10). *For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of Yahuah (Lord), make his paths straight.* (Matthew 3:3). Sirach is drawing on Malachi, *he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children* (Malachi 4:6), and then he says what Malachi's Elijah is for: to restore the tribes of Jacob. Not Yahudah (Judah) only, the tribes. That is the errand John steps into when he stands in the wilderness as the voice Isaiah heard, preparing the way of Yahuah (Lord). Preparing the way is the beginning of the Elijah work; the end of it is the scattered tribes of Jacob brought home, and the one whose way John prepared is the one who gathers them.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:10 — *to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.* The Elijah errand ends in the restoring of the tribes of Jacob; the voice in the wilderness at Matthew 3:3 is its beginning.

new_note: *Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:10). *And if ye will receive it, this is Elias, which was for to come.* (Matthew 11:14). When Yahusha (Jesus) says John is the Elias who was to come, he is pointing at a job description everyone in the crowd knew. Sirach had written it out: Elijah is ordained to reprove, to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob. All of Jacob, all twelve tribes, the scattered house of Yashar'el (Israel) and the house of Yahudah (Judah) together. John began that work at the Jordan; the full restoring of the tribes waits on the great and dreadful day Malachi set it beside (Malachi 4:5). *If ye will receive it* is the hard part, because receiving it means receiving that the gathering of a scattered people is what Elijah comes to do.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:10 — *to restore the tribes of Jacob.* Yahusha (Jesus) names John as Elias at Matthew 11:14, and Sirach says what Elijah comes to do: restore the tribes of Jacob, all twelve.

new_note: *Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God), before it brake forth into fury, and to turn the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:10). *And when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet.* (Matthew 14:5). Herod would have killed John and did not, because the people counted him a prophet. They were right, and more right than they knew. Sirach describes the prophet they were looking at: ordained for reproofs in his time, to hold back the wrath of judgment before it broke out, to turn the heart of the father to the son, to restore the tribes of Jacob. John reproved a king, called a nation to turn, and prepared the way for the one who gathers Jacob. Herod feared the crowd and not the Torah, and the crowd, for once, had the better instinct.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:10 — *Who were ordained for reproofs in their times, to pacify the wrath of the judgment of Yahuah (God).* The multitude at Matthew 14:5 counted John a prophet; Sirach describes which prophet, the Elijah ordained for reproofs and the restoring of Jacob.

new_note: *Blessed are they that saw you, and slept in love; for we shall surely live.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:11). *And his disciples came, and took up the body, and buried it, and went and told Yahusha (Jesus).* (Matthew 14:12). Sirach blesses the ones who saw Elijah and then fell asleep in love, and gives the reason in one line: for we shall surely live. Death is a sleep for the righteous, and the sleeper will wake. John's disciples saw the Elijah of their day, and when Herod took his head they took up his body and buried him, and then they went and told Yahusha (Jesus). They carried the news of the prophet's death to the one who holds the life Sirach was sure of. They had seen Elijah, they buried him in love, and they walked straight to the resurrection.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:11 — *Blessed are they that saw you, and slept in love; for we shall surely live.* John's disciples at Matthew 14:12 bury the Elijah of their day and go to Yahusha (Jesus), the one in whom we shall surely live.

new_note: *Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and Eliseus was filled with his spirit: while he lived, he was not moved with the presence of any prince, neither could any bring him into subjection.* (Ecclesiasticus 48:12). *Then cometh Yahusha (Jesus) from Galilee to Jordan unto John, to be baptized of him.* (Matthew 3:13). The whirlwind took Elijah at the Jordan, and Elisha came back across the same river carrying his spirit (2 Kings 2:8–15). Sirach adds that no prince could move Elijah while he lived. Now Yahusha (Jesus) comes from Galilee to the Jordan, to a man no prince could move either, the John who would shortly tell Herod his marriage was unlawful. At that river the heavens open and the Ruach HaKodesh (Holy Spirit) comes down on him (Matthew 3:16). The Jordan is where the prophetic spirit passed from Elijah to Elisha, and it is where the Spirit rests on the one Elijah's successor was sent to announce.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 48:12 — *Elias it was, who was covered with a whirlwind: and Eliseus was filled with his spirit.* The spirit passed from Elijah to Elisha at the Jordan; at Matthew 3:13 Yahusha (Jesus) comes to the same river and the Spirit descends.

new_note: *He stretched out his hand to the cup, and poured of the blood of the grape, he poured out at the foot of the altar a sweetsmelling savour to the most high King of all.* (Ecclesiasticus 50:15). *Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us.* (Hebrews 9:12). Simon the high priest finishes the altar service by pouring the blood of the grape at the foot of the altar, a sweet savour to the most high King. Yahusha (Jesus) took that same cup of the vine on his last night and said *this is my blood of the new testament* (Matthew 26:28). Hebrews says he then entered the holy place once, not with the blood of goats and calves but with his own. The wine poured at the altar's foot was showing in the fruit of the grape what the Messiah (Christ) would do in his own blood; Simon poured the picture, and the high priest after the order of Melek Tsadiq (Melchizedek) poured out the thing itself.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 50:15 — *poured of the blood of the grape, he poured out at the foot of the altar a sweetsmelling savour.* The blood of the grape at the altar's foot pictures what Hebrews 9:12 says the Messiah (Christ) did with his own blood, once.

new_note: *Draw near to me, you unlearned, and dwell in the house of learning.* (Ecclesiasticus 51:23). *Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.* (Matthew 11:28). Sirach ends his book with an invitation: draw near, you unlearned, and dwell in the house of learning. Yahusha (Jesus) issues the same one, come unto me, all you that labour and are heavy laden. Sirach was pointing people toward Wisdom; the one who speaks in Matthew is the Wisdom who stood beside the Maker before the world was (Ecclesiasticus 24:9; Proverbs 8:22–30), now speaking in his own voice. The load his hearers carried was the burden the scribes bound on them, *heavy burdens and grievous to be borne* (Matthew 23:4), not the Torah itself. The rest he offers is in the house of learning, not outside it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 51:23 — *Draw near to me, you unlearned, and dwell in the house of learning.* Sirach's closing invitation is the one Yahusha (Jesus) gives at Matthew 11:28; come near, and find the rest in the house of learning.

new_note: *Put your neck under the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction: she is hard at hand to find.* (Ecclesiasticus 51:26). *Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.* (Matthew 11:29). Sirach's yoke is instruction, and he tells the soul to receive it, so the rest he found was not rest from the yoke but rest under it. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same thing in the same order: take my yoke, learn of me, and you will find rest for your souls. He is quoting Jeremiah, *ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls* (Jeremiah 6:16). His yoke is not the absence of a yoke; it is the old path, his Father's commandments as he teaches and walks them, set in place of the heavy burdens the scribes had bound on men's shoulders (Matthew 23:4). Sirach put his neck under it and called it rest.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 51:26 — *Put your neck under the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction.* The yoke is the instruction and the rest is found under it, not away from it; Matthew 11:29 says take my yoke, learn of me.

new_note: *Behold with your eyes, how that I have but little labour, and have gotten to me much rest.* (Ecclesiasticus 51:27). *For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.* (Matthew 11:30). Sirach is not theorizing; he points to his own life and says look, little labour, much rest, and his neck is still under the yoke when he says it. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same of his yoke: easy, and the burden light. Neither man is describing a life without commandments. Moses said the commandment *is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off* (Deuteronomy 30:11), and John says *his commandments are not grievous* (1 John 5:3). The heavy thing was never the Torah; it was what men added to it, and the one who gave it carries it lightly.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 51:27 — *I have but little labour, and have gotten to me much rest.* Sirach's little labour and much rest under the yoke is Matthew 11:30, my yoke is easy and my burden is light.

new_note: *Work your work betimes, and in his time he will give you your reward.* (Ecclesiasticus 51:30). *His lord said unto him, Well done, good and faithful servant; thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.* (Matthew 25:23). Sirach's last word is a word about timing: do your work early, and the reward comes in his time, not yours. The faithful servant in the parable did exactly that; he worked while the master was away and was paid when the master came back, rule over many things and entry into his lord's joy. The reward is not handed out along the way. Yahusha (Jesus) says *the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works* (Matthew 16:27), and the reigning with him that follows the first resurrection is that reward (Revelation 20:4–6). The work is now; the wages are at his coming.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 51:30 — *Work your work betimes, and in his time he will give you your reward.* The reward comes in his time; at Matthew 25:23 the faithful servant receives it when the master returns, not before.

new_note: *Charging them to keep the passages of the hill country: for by them there was an entrance into Judea, and it was easy to stop them that would come up, because the passage was straight, for two men at the most.* (Judith 4:7). *For the ships of Chittim shall come against him: therefore he shall be grieved, and return, and have indignation against the holy covenant: so shall he do; he shall even return, and have intelligence with them that forsake the holy covenant.* (Daniel 11:30). Judith's Yashar'el (Israel) hears that the invader is coming and does two things: they hold the narrow passes into Judea, and they fast and cry to Yahuah (God) (Judith 4:9–13). Daniel describes the king such a people will keep facing, one whose indignation is against the holy covenant itself and who has intelligence with those inside who forsake it. The Maccabees would meet that king in Antiochus, and the pattern does not end there. The war is never only about the land; it is a war on the covenant, with help from the covenant's own deserters, and the people who keep it answer at the passes and on their knees.
member_note: Judith 4:7 — *it was easy to stop them that would come up, because the passage was straight.* The invader Judith's people brace for at the passes is the king of Daniel 11:30, whose indignation is against the holy covenant.

new_note: *For your power stands not in multitude nor your might in strong men: for you are a Yahuah (God) of the afflicted, an helper of the oppressed, an upholder of the weak, a protector of the forlorn, a saviour of them that are without hope.* (Judith 9:11). *But deliver us with yours hand, and help me that am desolate, and which have no other help but you.* (The Rest of Esther 14:14). Two women, two prayers, the same confession. Judith says Yahuah (God) is the helper of the oppressed and the saviour of those without hope, that his power never stood in numbers or strong men. Esther says it as a plea rather than a creed: deliver us with your hand, help me that am desolate, I have no other help but you. Each one stands alone in front of a power that means to wipe out her people, and each one knows the only hand that can turn it. The strength of Yashar'el (Israel) in both books is a woman on her knees who has run out of every other help.
member_note: Judith 9:11 — *a protector of the forlorn, a saviour of them that are without hope.* Esther prays the same thing at The Rest of Esther 14:14, no other help but you; two women alone before a power bent on their people.

new_note: *But the Almighty Yahuah (God) has disappointed them by the hand of a woman.* (Judith 16:6). *But Elohim (God) hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and Elohim (God) hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;* (1 Corinthians 1:27). The Almighty Yahuah (God) brought a whole army to nothing by the hand of one widow, and Judith's song says so without apology. Paul tells the Corinthians this is how Elohim (God) works on purpose: he chooses the weak things to confound the mighty and the foolish things to confound the wise, so that no flesh can glory in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:29). Holofernes bragged of what he would do to Yashar'el (Israel); the next verse of the song says the mighty one did not fall by young men or giants but by a woman. The hand of a woman is the weak thing, and the weak thing is what he chose.
member_note: Judith 16:6 — *the Almighty Yahuah (God) has disappointed them by the hand of a woman.* Yahuah (God) bringing an army to nothing by the hand of a widow is the weak confounding the mighty of 1 Corinthians 1:27.

new_note: *Let all creatures serve you: for you spakest, and they were made, you did send forth your spirit, and it created them, and there is none that can resist your voice.* (Judith 16:14). *Let them praise the name of Yahuah (LORD): for he commanded, and they were created.* (Psalm 148:5). Judith says the whole creation was made by speaking, you spoke and they were made, you sent forth your spirit and it created them. The psalm says the same of the heavens and the host of them: he commanded, and they were created, and that is why they are to praise his name. Moses wrote it as *Elohim (God) said, Let there be* with the Spirit moving on the waters (Genesis 1:2–3), and David wrote that *by the word of Yahuah (LORD) were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth* (Psalm 33:6). John names that Word: all things were made by him (John 1:3). What was made by a voice cannot resist that voice, and Judith says so.
member_note: Judith 16:14 — *for you spakest, and they were made, you did send forth your spirit, and it created them.* Creation by the spoken word; Psalm 148:5 calls all of it to praise the one who commanded, and they were created.

new_note: *From my youth up I have heard in the tribe of my family that you, O Yahuah (God), tookest Yashar'el (Israel) from among all people, and our fathers from all their predecessors, for a perpetual inheritance, and you have performed whatsoever you did promise them.* (The Rest of Esther 14:5). *For thou art an holy people unto Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God): Yahuah Elohayka (the LORD thy God) hath chosen thee to be a special people unto himself, above all people that are upon the face of the earth.* (Deuteronomy 7:6). Esther says she heard it in her youth, in the tribe of her family: Yahuah (God) took Yashar'el (Israel) from among all people for a perpetual inheritance. She is quoting Moses from memory in a Persian palace. Moses had said it to the whole people: chosen above all people on the face of the earth, a special people to himself. Esther is in exile, her people scattered under a foreign king and marked for slaughter, and nothing about that has cancelled what she heard in her tribe. A chosen people stays chosen in the lands of their scattering, and the inheritance is perpetual because the one who gave it does not take it back.
member_note: The Rest of Esther 14:5 — *tookest Yashar'el (Israel) from among all people, and our fathers from all their predecessors, for a perpetual inheritance.* Esther in exile recites what Moses said at Deuteronomy 7:6, a people chosen from among all people, and the choosing holds in the scattering.

new_note: *And now we have sinned before you: therefore have you given us into the hands of our enemies,* (The Rest of Esther 14:6). *And that I also have walked contrary unto them, and have brought them into the land of their enemies; if then their uncircumcised hearts be humbled, and they then accept of the punishment of their iniquity:* (Leviticus 26:41). Esther's prayer follows the lines Moses laid down. Leviticus 26 said that if the people broke the covenant, Yahuah (God) himself would walk contrary to them and bring them into the land of their enemies, and that the way back would open when their uncircumcised hearts were humbled and they accepted the punishment as just. Esther does exactly that: we have sinned, you gave us into our enemies' hands, you are righteous. The enemy's hand is the covenant curse at work, not the covenant's end, and the next line in Leviticus is the promise, *then will I remember my covenant with Jacob* (Leviticus 26:42). Her humbled heart in Persia is the turn the Torah said would bring them home.
member_note: The Rest of Esther 14:6 — *we have sinned before you: therefore have you given us into the hands of our enemies.* Esther prays inside Leviticus 26:41, the sin named, the enemy's hand owned as just, the humbled heart that turns the curse toward home.

new_note: *For into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter; nor dwell in the body that is subject to sin.* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4). *Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.* (Matthew 13:13). Wisdom will not move into a soul that is set against her. Yahusha (Jesus) speaks in parables for the same reason he gives in the next lines, quoting Isaiah: *this people's heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed* (Matthew 13:15). The parable did not shut them out; the closed eyes were their own doing, and wisdom does not force the door. In the same breath he tells the disciples their eyes are blessed because they see (Matthew 13:16). The teaching was one teaching; what differed was the soul it met.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 1:4 — *into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter.* Wisdom does not enter a soul set against her; at Matthew 13:13 the parables meet eyes that have closed themselves.

new_note: *Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret, that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul.* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:11). *But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.* (Matthew 12:36). Wisdom of Solomon says no word is so secret that it goes for nothing, and that a lying mouth kills the soul that owns it. Yahusha (Jesus) says every idle word will be accounted for in the day of judgment, and the next verse says what the accounting looks like: *by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned* (Matthew 12:37). Murmuring and backbiting feel like small, private sins. Both books say there is nothing private about them; the ear of jealousy hears everything, and the words are kept for the day.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 1:11 — *there is no word so secret, that shall go for nought.* No word goes for nothing; Matthew 12:36 says every idle word is accounted for in the day of judgment.

new_note: *Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret, that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul.* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:11). *For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:* (Matthew 15:19). Wisdom of Solomon warns about the mouth: murmuring, backbiting, the lying mouth that kills the soul. Yahusha (Jesus) traces the mouth back to its source, *those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart* (Matthew 15:18), and then lists what comes out of it, false witness and blasphemies among them. The two lists overlap because they are describing one thing from two ends: the heart is where the evil starts, and the tongue is where it shows. That is why the promise of the new covenant is a heart with the Torah written on it (Jeremiah 31:33), because a clean mouth needs a clean spring.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 1:11 — *the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul.* The lying mouth of Wisdom 1:11 and the false witness of Matthew 15:19 come from the same place, the heart.

new_note: *For Yahuah (God) made not death: neither has he pleasure in the destruction of the living.* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13). *And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* (Matthew 16:18). Wisdom of Solomon says it flatly: Yahuah (God) did not make death. It came in through the envy of the devil (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24) and through the sin in the garden; it is an intruder in his creation, not his design. That is why Yahusha (Jesus) can say the gates of hell, the gates of the grave, will not prevail against the assembly he builds. A thing the Father did not make has no permanent claim on what he did make. The grave's gates held every son of Adam until the one who said this walked out through them on the third day, and because he did, the gates will not hold his people either.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 1:13 — *Yahuah (God) made not death: neither has he pleasure in the destruction of the living.* Death is not of Yahuah's (God's) making, so the gates of the grave at Matthew 16:18 have no lasting claim on the assembly he builds.

new_note: *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12). *That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying, Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses.* (Matthew 8:17). Wisdom of Solomon 2 is a long portrait of the righteous one hunted by the ungodly, from the lying in wait here to the shameful death they plan for him in verse 20. Isaiah painted the same man: despised, a man of sorrows, bearing our griefs and carrying our sorrows (Isaiah 53:3–4). Matthew says the healings fulfil that line; the one carrying away the sicknesses of Capernaum is the servant Isaiah saw. He is also the righteous one of Wisdom 2, and the reason the ungodly hate him is given here: his life reproves their breaking of the law. The one who bore our sicknesses was, at the same time, being watched by men who wanted him dead for being righteous.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 — *let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn.* The righteous one of Wisdom 2 is Isaiah's servant; at Matthew 8:17 he bears our sicknesses while the ungodly lie in wait for him.

new_note: *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12). *The Son of Adam came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children.* (Matthew 11:19). The system faulted John for fasting and Yahusha (Jesus) for eating, which tells you the complaints were not the reason. Wisdom of Solomon gave the reason long before: the righteous one is clean contrary to our doings and upbraids us with our offending the law, so let us lie in wait for him. The glutton and winebibber charge is a cover for the grievance the ungodly admit among themselves, that his life exposes their departure from the Torah. *Wisdom is justified of her children* because wisdom's own book had already written the accusers' script.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 — *he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law.* The contradictory complaints of Matthew 11:19 hide the real grievance Wisdom 2:12 names: the righteous one reproves their lawbreaking.

new_note: *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12). *For Herod had laid hold on John, and bound him, and put him in prison for Herodias’ sake, his brother Philip’s wife.* (Matthew 14:3). John upbraided Herod with his offending the law, *it is not lawful for thee to have her* (Matthew 14:4), and Herod laid hold on him and bound him. That is Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 acted out at a king's court: the righteous one is clean contrary to what the king is doing, his word reproves the king's bed, and so the king and the woman lie in wait for him. The same reflex shows up wherever a righteous man reproves a system that has left the Torah, in the Pharisees who take counsel to destroy Yahusha (Jesus) (Matthew 12:14) and in the chief priests who do the same (Matthew 26:3–4). Herod is one more instance of a very old disposition.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 — *he upbraideth us with our offending the law.* John upbraids Herod with the law at Matthew 14:3–4 and is bound for it, the ungodly lying in wait for the righteous.

new_note: *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12). *From that time forth began Yahusha (Jesus) to shew unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day.* (Matthew 16:21). The ungodly in Wisdom of Solomon 2 begin by lying in wait and end by resolving, *let us condemn him with a shameful death* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:20). Yahusha (Jesus) tells his disciples the same ending in advance, suffering at the hands of the elders, chief priests and scribes, and death in Jerusalem. The religious leadership of the day fills the role Wisdom wrote for the ungodly, a system that could not bear a righteous man whose life reproved it. But he adds a line Wisdom's plotters never saw coming, raised again the third day, and Wisdom itself knew it: the souls of the righteous are in the hand of Elohim (God) (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1).
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 — *let us lie in wait for the righteous.* The plot of Wisdom 2 ends in a shameful death; at Matthew 16:21 Yahusha (Jesus) names the same end and adds the third day.

new_note: *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:12). *Judas then, having received a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons.* (John 18:3). The arrest at night is the lying in wait. Judas comes with a band of men and officers sent by the chief priests and Pharisees, with lanterns and torches and weapons, for one unarmed man in a garden. Wisdom of Solomon had already named the motive: the righteous one is clean contrary to their doings and upbraids them with their offending the law. The plot against the righteous one is not a New Testament novelty; the ungodly had been lying in wait for the just man who reproves them for as long as there have been just men, and the torches in Gethsemane are that old resolve carried out.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:12 — *Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous.* The band with lanterns and torches at John 18:3 is the lying in wait of the ungodly for the righteous one who reproves them.

new_note: *He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:13). *And when the tempter came to him, he said, If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), command that these stones be made bread.* (Matthew 4:3). The ungodly in Wisdom of Solomon fasten on one claim, that the righteous man calls himself the child of Yahuah (God), and they set out to test it: *if the just man be the son of Yahuah (God), he will help him* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18). The tempter in the wilderness uses the same handle, if you are the Son of Elohim (God), prove it, command the stones. The test comes back at the cross in the same words, *If thou be the Son of Elohim (God), come down from the cross* (Matthew 27:40). The claim of sonship is what the ungodly cannot leave alone, and the devil was the first to pick it up.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:13 — *he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* The ungodly test the righteous one's claim to be the child of Yahuah (God); the tempter at Matthew 4:3 says if thou be the Son.

new_note: *He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:13). *For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother.* (Matthew 12:50). The righteous one in Wisdom of Solomon calls himself the child of Yahuah (God), and two verses later the ungodly say why they believe him enough to hate him: his life is not like other men's, his ways are of another fashion. Yahusha (Jesus) names the family of the Father the same way, whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother, sister, mother. The child of Yahuah (God) is known by a life that does the Father's will; that is how the Father's children are recognised. The ungodly recognised it too, and it was the recognising that made them lie in wait.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:13 — *He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* The child of Yahuah (God) is known by a life of another fashion; Matthew 12:50 says the same, whoever does the will of my Father.

new_note: *He professeth to have the knowledge of Yahuah (God): and he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* (Wisdom of Solomon 2:13). *The Yahudim (Jews) answered him, We have a law, and by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of Elohim (God).* (John 19:7). The charge the accusers bring to Pilate, *by our law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of Elohim (God)*, is word for word the complaint Wisdom of Solomon put in the mouth of the ungodly against the righteous one: he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God). What the plotters of Wisdom 2 treat as the offence worth killing for is what the chief priests treat as the capital offence at the trial. They did not invent the charge; they inherited it from men who had been laying in wait for the righteous since before there was a Pilate to bring it to. And the law they appealed to was the law his life had been reproving them with.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 2:13 — *he calls himself the child of Yahuah (God).* The capital charge of John 19:7, he made himself the Son of Elohim (God), is the complaint Wisdom 2:13 gives the ungodly.
